summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual sexual conduct between men and carries a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust's country profile, Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 (covering events of 2023) and the UK Home Office's country-policy and information note of July 2024 all record the offence as in force. The Home Office documents cases prosecuted under Article 120 between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant; 2023 is the most recent documented case in this record.

Uzbekistan has no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor remains, in law, the sex assigned at birth, and Human Dignity Trust notes that transgender people may be prosecuted under Article 120 on that basis. Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment, and the Home Office describes police intimidation, violence and exploitation of gay men and trans people as routine.

Forced examinations of detainees amount to torture, according to the World Health Organization as cited by Human Rights Watch, which also records continuing impunity for police ill-treatment. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records torture and ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody alongside social stigma and violence against LGBT people under the criminalised framework.

The US State Department's 2023 report documents a specific enforcement pattern: LGBTQI+ people arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest unless they paid bribes, and police coercing LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2021 that gay and bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no protection, and urged decriminalisation.

Official hostility is on the record. In April 2023 the Constitution of Uzbekistan explicitly included gender, race, religion and nationality as protected categories while deliberately omitting sexual orientation. In November 2024 the leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party, Alisher Qodirov, announced he was drafting a law banning discussions of LGBTQ people, stating it was inspired by statements about "LGBT propaganda" in schools made by Ivanka Trump.
tangentialFactors:
The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence statistic for Uzbekistan, and none is carried here: without a figure set against the country's general homicide rate, a raw count would say nothing about trans-specific risk.

The US State Department reports are country-wide human rights assessments in which LGBT issues form one section, so their framing is broader than trans visitors' exposure. Human Rights Watch's March 2021 appeal for decriminalisation was made while Uzbekistan held a seat on the UN Human Rights Council, an institutional position that did not change the operation of Article 120.

The Home Office note attributes much of the discrimination outside state custody to a rural taboo, which distinguishes urban and rural exposure in a way the national legal picture alone does not.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in Uzbekistan and operate unofficially, according to the UK Home Office's July 2024 note, leaving residents without a formal protection or advocacy machinery.

Residents face coercion into informing on others: the US State Department's 2023 report records police compelling LGBTQI+ people to denounce acquainters under threat of prison, alongside arrest-and-release cycles used to extract bribes.

Societal harassment continued per the 2023 report, and websites and bloggers self-censored on LGBTQI+ issues. The absence of legal gender recognition means residents cannot obtain documents matching their gender identity, and the April 2023 constitutional text gives them no sexual-orientation-based ground of protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
ECOM's 2024 national report on Uzbekistan covers legislation, anti-discrimination provisions, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the rights to health and to work, but the inventory supplies no specific findings from it; those particulars remain unresolved here.

The inventory carries no sourced position on hate-crime provisions, access to gender-affirming care, bathroom or facilities rules, or entry and document-screening treatment of trans travellers at Uzbekistan's border. Whether any of these exist in domestic law is not established by the sources listed.

The November 2024 announcement by Alisher Qodirov concerns a bill he said he was drafting; the inventory does not record its passage, so its current legislative status is unresolved.
